An indication is a sign, signal, or piece of information that points you toward something — something that exists, is likely to happen, or should be done. Think of it as a pointer. It says, in effect: "look here" or "this is what's going on."
The Single Most Important Thing to Understand

An indication suggests something — it does not prove it.

This is the heart of the word. An indication points toward a conclusion and makes it likely, but it leaves room for doubt. It is not a guarantee.

Here's a simple example: Dark clouds are an indication that it might rain. The clouds strongly suggest rain — but they don't guarantee it. The rain may never arrive. That gap between pointing toward something and proving it is exactly where the word "indication" lives.

This is also why you'll often see words like clear, strong, good, or early placed in front of it — because by itself, an indication is never absolute certainty, and these modifiers tell you how convincing the sign is.

1. A sign that something is happening, exists, or is true

This is the most common use. An indication is a visible, noticeable, or measurable sign that reveals something about a situation, person, or thing.

A cough can be an indication of a cold. A sudden drop in a company's stock price is an indication that something is going wrong internally. His trembling hands were a clear indication of how nervous he was. In each case, one thing (the sign) is pointing you toward another thing (the reality behind it).

2. A hint about something that hasn't been stated directly

Sometimes a person doesn't say something openly but gives off clues through their behavior, silence, tone, or words. Those clues are indications.

"She gave no indication that she was planning to leave" means she never said it, and she never behaved in a way that suggested it either. "His silence was an indication that he disagreed" means his not speaking communicated something, even without words. Here, an indication is an indirect signal — something you read between the lines.

3. A rough idea or approximate sense of something

Sometimes "indication" means an early signal or a general direction — not a precise answer, but enough to give you a reasonable sense of things.

"The survey gives us a good indication of how people feel about the new policy" — it doesn't capture every person's exact truth, but it gives a reliable general picture. "Early test results gave the doctors an indication of what might be wrong" — the results pointed them in a direction, even if the full picture wasn't yet clear. In this sense, an indication is like a first draft of the truth.

4. A medical meaning — a reason to use a specific treatment

In medicine and pharmacology, "indication" has a precise technical meaning. A medical indication is a condition, symptom, or situation that makes a particular treatment, drug, or procedure appropriate or recommended.

High blood pressure is an indication for prescribing certain medications — meaning the presence of high blood pressure is a medically recognized reason to use those drugs. Chest pain is an indication for running an ECG test — meaning it justifies ordering that test. The word is used to establish that there is a legitimate medical reason behind a clinical decision.

The opposite term in medicine is a contraindication — a reason not to use a treatment (for example, being pregnant is a contraindication for certain drugs).
How It Compares to Similar Words

Indication vs. Proof — Proof closes the case. It confirms something with certainty, leaving no room for doubt. An indication only points in a direction — you can have strong indications of something and still be wrong. You cannot have genuine proof of something and be wrong.

Indication vs. Symptom — A symptom is mostly a medical or physical word — a headache, a fever, a rash. Indication is far broader and works in any domain: business, science, conversation, behavior, test results, and more. In medicine, symptoms can be indications, but outside medicine, the word "symptom" sounds odd whereas "indication" sounds natural.

Indication vs. Hint — A hint is usually subtle and often deliberate — someone drops a hint on purpose. An indication can be intentional or unintentional, obvious or subtle.

Indication vs. Clue — A clue carries a flavor of investigation or mystery-solving. Indication is more neutral and works equally well in formal writing, everyday speech, scientific reports, and medical records.

"Give an indication of" — to show, suggest, or signal something. "Can you give me an indication of the timeline?"

"No indication" — no sign or evidence at all. "There was no indication that anything was wrong."

"A clear indication" — an obvious, hard-to-miss sign. "The falling sales are a clear indication of a deeper problem."

"A strong indication" — a very convincing sign, though still short of proof. "The test results are a strong indication that the treatment is working."

"Every indication" — all available signs point the same way. "Every indication suggests the project will be a success."

"Early indications" — the first signs of something, before the full picture is available. "Early indications suggest the vaccine is safe."

"Is there any indication...?" — a common question asking whether any signs exist. "Is there any indication of when he'll arrive?"

The word "indication" is fundamentally about inference — drawing a conclusion from a sign rather than from direct, confirmed knowledge. Whenever you use or see this word, the underlying logic is always: "This sign points toward that reality, though it does not prove it with absolute certainty." Once you hold that core idea, the word will make sense in every context you encounter it.
